transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Come in, Daniel. I've read your essay on social media and news, and I wanted to give you some feedback.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Thanks, Dr Brown. I hope it wasn't too bad.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Not at all. You chose an interesting topic, and your introduction is strong. You explain clearly why people now get news from their phones.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: That's good to hear. I spent the most time on that part.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: It shows. However, the main problem is the structure of your second section. You jump between three different ideas, and it's hard to follow your argument.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I see. I wasn't sure how to organise the examples.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: My suggestion is to give each idea its own paragraph, and to start every paragraph with a clear topic sentence. For example, one paragraph for fake news, one for young readers, one for advertising.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: That makes sense. What about my sources?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: You have eight sources, which is fine, but three of them are blogs. For an academic essay you should use journals, books or reliable news sites.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Oh. I didn't know blogs were a problem.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: They can be useful for opinions, but they're not strong evidence. Try to replace at least two of them.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Your conclusion is rather short, only three sentences. It should summarise your main points and say what you think the future of news will be.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I ran out of time. The deadline was very close.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: I understand, but remember: you have a chance to improve it. The final version is due on the twentieth of March, and it's worth forty per cent of your mark.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Thanks. I'll start rewriting tonight. Can I send you the new draft before I hand it in?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Of course. Send it by the fifteenth and I'll check it quickly. Also, think about adding one short example from a recent news story. It will make your argument more convincing, and it will help you reach a better mark.
